title: Metal Rhythm
goal: Play a tight palm-muted riff with power chords, gallops and a pedal tone, at tempo with a band and for a full minute.
assumes: You can play eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM and fret a note on the low strings cleanly. An electric guitar with some distortion helps, but every Exercise works clean. The minutes listed are one pass through the material; expect to come back to each Step for days or weeks.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM
Clean single notes on the low strings

orderRationale: The palm mute and the downstroke first, because every later riff is made of them. Power chords next, then the two together, which is already a riff, and then the same chug and chords from the A string, so later riffs can use both low strings. The gallop and its reverse are the same three notes with one stroke left out, so they come before continuous sixteenths, where no stroke is left out and the hand has to alternate. Chord changes under the gallop close that Level, once the picking hand no longer needs watching. Triplets and bursts, pedal riffs that leave the low string, pedal riffs from the A string, a riff that joins a pedal part to a gallop part, and the long takes come last because they need the stamina the earlier Steps build. The Path ends on a verse and a chorus played over the band as a sixteen-bar form.
gradingLimits: The app times each attack and counts the ones it heard. A two-note power chord is one attack: it is timed and counted, and its pitch is not checked. Palm muting and the direction of each stroke are taught here and cannot be heard apart, so they are yours to keep honest. Heavy distortion and compression blur where a note starts; for a graded take, turn the gain down to a crunch, or use the dry signal if your interface has one. Sixteenths above 150 BPM are close to the fastest the app will grade. None of this has been tried on a real guitar yet.

steps.title: The chug
steps.goal: Play palm-muted eighth notes on a low string in downstrokes, every one the same weight, and lift the mute for an accent.
steps.why: The palm-muted downstroke is the sound of metal rhythm guitar. It is two skills at once: the picking hand mutes and plays in the same place, and the stroke only ever goes down, so the hand has to come back up between every note without being heard.
howTo: Rest the side of the picking hand on the strings right where they leave the bridge. Too far forward and the note dies; too far back and it rings. Find the spot where it thuds and still has a pitch.
Every note is a downstroke. Play from the wrist, small, and let the hand bounce back up by itself.
For an accent, lift the palm a little so the string rings, and bring it straight back.
steps.payoff: A two-bar riff on the low E string that thuds evenly and opens up where you choose.

exercises.title: Eight to the bar
exercises.purpose: Palm-muted eighths on an open low string, the low E or the A, all downstrokes, with two fretted notes at the end of the second bar. The sound comes first: get the mute right before you worry about speed.
howTo: Eighth notes, two to the click, all down. The last two notes are frets 3 and 5, muted like the rest.
Listen to each note. They should all be as short and as loud as each other, like a machine.
exercises.coachLine: I time every stroke and say how even they were. The mute and the direction of the strokes are for you to judge.
selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?
Were they all downstrokes, to the last bar?

exercises.title: Muted and open
exercises.purpose: The chug with fretted notes let out of the mute: G, A and the Bb that makes it sound heavy. The palm has to lift and come back inside an eighth note.
howTo: Mute the open E notes and let the fretted notes ring: lift the palm just enough as you play them.
First finger on fret 3, third on fret 5, little finger on fret 6. All downstrokes.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.
selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?

exercises.title: Accents in threes
exercises.purpose: The open E string with the mute lifted on every third eighth: 3 + 3 + 2. The accents make the riff; bar 2 ends on two accented fretted notes.
howTo: Lift the palm for the accented notes and dig in a little more. Mute everything else.
Count '1 2 3, 1 2 3, 1 2'. In bar 2 the last two accents are frets 3 and 5.
exercises.coachLine: Accents are measured roughly: louder than the notes either side or not. With heavy gain they flatten out, so try this one with less.

notes: Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

steps.title: Power chords
steps.goal: Play two-note power chords on the low strings, move them without a gap, and stop them dead.
steps.why: A power chord is a root and the note a fifth above it, on two neighbouring strings. It has no major or minor in it, which is why it stays clear under distortion. The shape never changes, so the work is in moving it in time and in silencing it.
howTo: First finger on the root, third finger two frets up on the next string. For E, the low E string is open and the first finger takes fret 2 of the A string.
Let the first finger lie lightly across the higher strings so they can't ring, and hit only the two strings of the chord.
To stop a chord, relax the fretting fingers without lifting them off the strings, and lay the picking hand down at the same time.
steps.payoff: Three chords, E, G and A, that move in time and stop as one.

exercises.title: E, G and A
exercises.purpose: E, G and A in quarter notes, two strokes on each, and back to G to finish. Slow enough to land both fingers at once and hear both strings.
howTo: E: open low E and fret 2 on the A string. G: fret 3 and fret 5. A: fret 5 and fret 7. Downstrokes through both strings.
Move the hand as one shape. The fingers keep their spacing while the hand slides.
exercises.coachLine: A chord is one attack to me: I time it and count it, and I don't check its pitch.
selfCheck: Did both strings of every chord sound, and no others?

exercises.title: Chords and stops
exercises.purpose: Eighth-note chords with rests between them. The silence has to be as tight as the chord, or the riff turns to mush.
howTo: Count '1 and, (2) and, (3) and 4, (and)'. Stop the strings with both hands on each rest.
All downstrokes. The hand keeps moving in eighths through the rests.
exercises.coachLine: I time each chord. A sound in a rest counts as an extra note; strings left humming are for your ear.
selfCheck: On a recording, do the stops sound silent, with nothing ringing through them?

exercises.title: A riff in fifths
exercises.purpose: E held for a beat, then G and A as eighths, a rest, and round again: a riff made of nothing but power chords.
howTo: The hand jumps from the open E shape to fret 3. Go early: leave the E chord a hair before the beat is over.
Keep the first and third fingers on their strings as the shape slides between G and A.
exercises.coachLine: The jump from E to G is where a chord arrives late. I'll say how even it was.

steps.difficultyException: Chords in quarters, and in eighths with rests between them, after eight chugs to the bar; a two-note chord is one attack, so the rate falls. The demand is both fingers landing as one shape and both strings stopping together, which the metric does not count.

steps.title: Chug against chord
steps.goal: Switch between muted single notes and ringing power chords inside one bar, all in downstrokes.
steps.why: This is the riff every heavy band plays: a muted low string chugging, and chords punching out of it. The picking hand has to change from one muted string to two open ones and back in an eighth note, and the contrast between the two is the whole effect.
howTo: Muted notes: one string, palm down, small stroke. Chords: palm up, a bigger stroke through two strings.
Keep the fretting hand's shape hovering over the next chord while the open string chugs.
Loud chords, quiet chug. If they sound the same, exaggerate the difference until they don't.
steps.payoff: A riff that sounds like a record: chug, chug, chord.

exercises.title: E chord out of the chug
exercises.purpose: The 3 + 3 + 2 accents again, but each accent is now a ringing E power chord and the notes between are muted.
howTo: First finger stays on fret 2 of the A string until the last beat of bar 2. On the accents, lift the palm and strike both strings.
Bar 2 ends with G and A chords on the last two eighths.
exercises.coachLine: I check that the chords were louder than the chug, roughly, and how even the time was.

notes: Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: Chords on the move
exercises.purpose: Two muted notes, a G chord, two muted notes, an A chord: the chords change while the chug stays on the open string.
howTo: In bar 1 the fretting hand has two muted notes to get to each chord: move during them. In bar 2 the A and G chords come back to back.
The last chord of bar 2 is an E held for a beat. Let it ring.
exercises.coachLine: I time every attack, chug and chord alike, and say how even they were.
selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?

exercises.title: Chug, chord, stop
exercises.purpose: The same idea with holes in it: a rest after the G chord and after the A. Three sounds now, muted, open and silent.
howTo: Count '1 and 2 and, (3) and 4, (and)'. Kill the chord with both hands on each rest.
Don't let the rest shorten. The attack after it, a chug in bar 1 and the A chord in bar 2, comes on the 'and', not before.
exercises.coachLine: The note after each rest is the one I'd look at: early is the usual mistake.
selfCheck: On a recording, do the stops sound silent, with nothing ringing through them?

steps.title: The chug from the A string
steps.goal: Play the palm-muted chug on the open A string, play A, C and D power chords with their roots on the A string, and put a low E chug under those chords in one riff.
steps.why: So far every chord has had its root on the low E string, and the A string has only had the plain chug to itself. The same chug and the same chord shape work one string higher, and a riff can use both strings at once. Nothing here is new for the picking hand except where it sits: the mute has to be found again on a thinner string, and the low E string, which now lies next to the pick without being played, has to stay silent.
howTo: Move the side of the picking hand so it lies on the A string where the string leaves the bridge. It rests on the low E string too, and that keeps the low E string quiet.
Begin each downstroke on the A string itself, not above it. For a chord, lift the palm and carry the stroke through the A and D strings only.
The chord shape is the one you know: first finger on the root, third finger two frets up on the next string. For A, the A string is open and the first finger takes fret 2 of the D string.
steps.payoff: A riff with a muted low E string under chords on the A string, and a chug that is at home on two strings.

exercises.title: Muted and open on the A string
exercises.purpose: The chug on the open A string with fretted notes let out of the mute: C, D and E flat on frets 3, 5 and 6. The same move as on the low E string, with the mute found again on a thinner string.
howTo: Eighth notes, two to the click, all downstrokes. Mute the open A notes and let the fretted notes ring: lift the palm just enough as you play them.
First finger on fret 3, third on fret 5, little finger on fret 6, all on the A string. Bar 1 lets out fret 3 and then fret 5. Bar 2 lets out fret 3 and ends on frets 5, 6, 5, 3.
The low E string is not played. Begin every stroke on the A string.
exercises.coachLine: Every note is timed, and after the take the notes are checked against the written ones. The mute, the direction of the strokes and a quiet low E string are yours to judge.
selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?
Did the low E string stay silent from the first bar to the last?

exercises.title: A, C and D
exercises.purpose: A, C and D power chords with their roots on the A string: the shapes of E, G and A, one string higher. Quarter notes in bar 1, eighth notes in bar 2.
howTo: A: the open A string and fret 2 on the D string. C: fret 3 on the A string and fret 5 on the D string. D: fret 5 and fret 7. Downstrokes through both strings.
Bar 1 is quarter notes: A twice, C twice. Bar 2 is eighth notes: D four times, then C four times.
Begin every stroke on the A string itself, so the low E string is never touched.
exercises.coachLine: A chord is one attack: it is timed and counted, and its pitch is not checked. Whether only the A and D strings sounded is yours to judge.
selfCheck: Did both strings of every chord sound, and no others?

exercises.title: Chords out of the A chug
exercises.purpose: Three plus three plus two from the A string: a chord, two muted open A notes, a chord, two more, a chord and one. Bar 1 has A, C and D; bar 2 has A and D, and ends on two C chords.
howTo: Eighth notes, all downstrokes. Muted notes: one string, palm down, small stroke. Chords: palm up, a bigger stroke through the A and D strings.
Bar 1 is A, C, D with two muted notes after the A and the C and one after the D. Bar 2 is A, D, and then C twice to end the bar.
The fretting hand has two muted notes to get to each C and D chord. Keep its fingers off the A string while the open string chugs, and hover over the next chord.
After the A chord, lift the first finger off the D string so the chord does not ring on over the chug.
exercises.coachLine: Every attack is timed, chug and chord alike, and the evenness is reported. A chord's pitch is not checked, and the mute is yours to judge.
selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?
Did the low E string stay silent from the first bar to the last?

exercises.title: Low E chug, A-string chords
exercises.purpose: A riff on both low strings: the muted chug goes back to the open low E string and the chords stay on the A string. Two chugs and a chord, through A, C, D and C, with four chugs in a row over the bar line, to an A held for a beat.
howTo: Eighth notes, all downstrokes. Bar 1: two chugs, A, two chugs, C, two chugs. Bar 2: two chugs, D, two chugs, C, and A held for a beat.
The pick changes string for every chord. Begin the chord's stroke on the A string, so the low E string does not ring under it, and bring the palm back down for the chug.
The last chord is the open A string and fret 2 of the D string. Let it ring for the whole beat.
exercises.coachLine: Every attack is timed, chug and chord alike, and the evenness is reported. A chord's pitch is not checked; the mute and which strings rang are yours to judge.
selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?
Did each chord sound on the A and D strings only, with the low E string quiet under it?

steps.title: The gallop
steps.goal: Play the gallop, an eighth and two sixteenths, evenly on a muted string and against chords.
steps.why: The gallop is the rhythm of classic heavy metal. It is three strokes to a beat, down, down-up, and the trouble is the two short ones: they bunch up against the next beat unless the hand keeps a steady sixteenth-note swing underneath.
howTo: Count '1, and a, 2, and a'. Down on the beat, then down-up on the 'and a'.
The hand swings in sixteenths the whole time and misses the string once a beat, on the 'e'.
Stay palm-muted and keep the strokes small. The gallop gets its sound from being tight, not loud.
steps.payoff: A galloping riff on the low E string that holds its shape as the tempo climbs.

exercises.title: The gallop on one string
exercises.purpose: Eight gallops on one muted low string, the low E or the A, the last two on frets 3 and 5. Nothing to think about except the three strokes.
howTo: Down, down-up, on every beat. The long note is on the click.
If the two short notes sound like one smeared note, slow down a rung until you can hear both.
exercises.coachLine: I time all three notes of every beat and say how even they were. The strokes are yours to keep.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?

exercises.title: A chord, then the gallop
exercises.purpose: A power chord on beat 1 of bar 1, and on beats 1 and 3 of bar 2, with the gallop carrying on underneath on the open string.
howTo: The chord takes the place of the gallop's long note: chord, then the two short muted notes, then a full gallop.
E, then G and A in the second bar. Lift the palm for the chord and drop it straight back.
exercises.coachLine: I time every attack and say how even they were. A chord's pitch is not something I check.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: A galloping riff
exercises.purpose: Two gallops, two open eighth notes that climb, and a gallop to answer; the second bar ends on a long note. E blues on one string.
howTo: The eighth notes on frets 3, 5 and 6 are open, not muted, and all downstrokes: first finger on 3, third on 5, little finger on 6.
Keep the sixteenth-note swing going through the eighths, so the next gallop starts in time.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: The reverse gallop
steps.goal: Play two sixteenths and an eighth, bursts of four sixteenths, and change between them and the gallop.
steps.why: Turn the gallop round and the short notes come first: down-up, down. It feels like a different rhythm and it trips players who learned the gallop as a reflex. Riffs mix the two, and a burst of four sixteenths between eighths, so each has to be a choice.
howTo: Count '1 e and, 2 e and'. Down-up on the '1 e', down on the 'and'.
The first short note is on the click. Don't let the pair fall early, before the beat.
For four sixteenths and two eighths, count '1 e and a, 2 and': down-up-down-up, down, down.
steps.payoff: A riff with both gallops in it, played without having to think which is which.

exercises.title: Short-short-long
exercises.purpose: Eight reverse gallops on one muted low string, the low E or the A, the last two on frets 3 and 5.
howTo: Down-up, down, on every beat. The hand misses the string on the 'a'.
Give the first note of each beat a little weight so you can hear where the beat is.
exercises.coachLine: I time all three notes of every beat and say how even they were.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Four fast, two slow
exercises.purpose: A beat of four muted sixteenths and a beat of two eighths, twice a bar. The eighths at the end of each bar are fretted and open.
howTo: The sixteenths alternate, down-up-down-up. The eighths are both downstrokes.
The eighths are exactly half the speed of the sixteenths. Players nearly always rush them.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Both gallops in one riff
exercises.purpose: A gallop, a reverse gallop, a gallop, and two open eighths; then the answer, ending on a long note.
howTo: Say it first: '1, and a, 2 e and, 3, and a, 4 and'.
The hand swings in sixteenths from start to finish. Only which strokes touch the string changes.
exercises.coachLine: This is the Step's test piece. I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: Sixteenths, alternate picked
steps.goal: Play a bar of continuous palm-muted sixteenths with strict down-up strokes, and put accents and fretted notes into it.
steps.why: Past a certain tempo downstrokes run out and the hand has to alternate. Muted sixteenths on one string are where that starts: the upstroke has to be as heavy as the downstroke, under a palm mute, which is harder than it sounds because the pick meets the string from the other side.
howTo: Strict alternation: down on the beat and the 'and', up on the 'e' and the 'a'. Never two the same way.
Angle the pick a little so it slides through the string in both directions.
Accents are made by lifting the palm, on whichever stroke they fall.
steps.payoff: A sixteenth-note riff with a melody poking out of the chug.

exercises.title: Sixteen to the bar
exercises.purpose: Two bars of muted sixteenths on an open low string, the low E or the A, with the mute lifted on the first note of every beat.
howTo: Down-up-down-up, four to the click. Lift the palm slightly on each beat's first note.
Listen to the upstrokes. If they are thinner than the downstrokes, slow down and even them out.
exercises.coachLine: I check that the first note of each beat was louder, roughly, and how even the sixteenths were.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.
Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: Threes across the beat
exercises.purpose: The same sixteen notes with an accent every three: five accents a bar, and two of them fall on upstrokes.
howTo: Count the sixteenths '1 2 3, 1 2 3, 1 2 3, 1 2 3, 1 2 3 4'. The picking never changes; only the palm does.
Tap your foot on the beat and let the accents pull against it.
exercises.coachLine: The accents on the upstrokes are the test. The accent readout is rough, so trust your ear too.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.
Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: A melody out of the chug
exercises.purpose: Sixteenths on the low E string where one note in four is fretted and open: G, A and Bb come up out of the muted pedal.
howTo: First finger on fret 3, third on fret 5, little finger on fret 6. Lift the palm for the fretted notes.
Strict down-up. Nearly every fretted note falls on a downstroke; the very last note of bar 2 is on an upstroke.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: Gallops through chord changes
steps.goal: Keep the gallop and the reverse gallop even while the chord under them changes, first every bar and then every two beats.
steps.why: So far the gallop has mostly sat on the open string while a chord or two went by. In a riff with a progression the gallop follows the chords: each chord gets its own galloping root, and the fretting hand has to move the shape without the picking hand waiting for it. A gap or a rushed beat at the change is the usual fault, and the figures themselves are the ones you already have.
howTo: Each chord has its root on one low string. On the low E string, E is the open string, G is fret 3, A is fret 5 and C is fret 8; other Takes play the same frets on the A string, which makes them A, C, D and F.

Play the three fretted chords with the first and third fingers. The chord on the open string needs only the first finger, on fret 2 of the next string. Keep the shape down while you gallop on its root, palm-muted.
The strokes are the ones you know: down, down-up for the gallop, and down-up, down for the reverse gallop. The picking hand swings in sixteenths and never waits.
Start moving the fretting hand on the last note before a change, and let that note be a little short if it has to be. A short note is better than a late chord.
steps.payoff: A galloping riff that carries four chords, with the click and then with a band.

exercises.title: The gallop, a chord to a bar
exercises.purpose: Four bars, one chord each: E, G, A and C. Every bar starts with its power chord, gallops on that chord's root, and ends on two eighth notes.
howTo: The chord takes the place of the first gallop's long note: chord and two short muted notes on beat 1, a full gallop on beat 2 and another on beat 3, and two muted eighth notes on beat 4. Down, down-up, and two downstrokes to end the bar.
E gallops on the open low E string, G on fret 3, A on fret 5 and C on fret 8, each fretted root under the first finger. Lift the palm for the chord and drop it straight back.
The last eighth note of the bar is where the fretting hand moves. Let that note be short and land the next chord on the click.
exercises.coachLine: Every attack is timed, chord and gallop alike, and the evenness is reported. A chord's pitch is not checked; the mute and the strokes are yours to judge.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?

variants.label: A string
variants.purpose: Four bars, one chord each: A, C, D and F, with their roots on the A string. Every bar starts with its power chord, gallops on that chord's root, and ends on two eighth notes.
howTo: The chord takes the place of the first gallop's long note: chord and two short muted notes on beat 1, a full gallop on beat 2 and another on beat 3, and two muted eighth notes on beat 4. Down, down-up, and two downstrokes to end the bar.
The A bar gallops on the open A string, C on fret 3, D on fret 5 and F on fret 8, each fretted root under the first finger. Lift the palm for the chord and drop it straight back.
The last eighth note of the bar is where the fretting hand moves. Let that note be short and land the next chord on the click.
The low E string is not played. Begin every stroke on the A string and let the palm keep the low E string quiet.

exercises.title: The reverse gallop, a chord to a bar
exercises.purpose: E, G, A and C again, now under the reverse gallop, a bar each. The short notes are muted on the root, and on beats 2 and 4 the long note is the chord.
howTo: Count '1 e and, 2 e and'. Beats 1 and 3 are short-short-long on the muted root. On beats 2 and 4 the long note is the chord: lift the palm and strike both strings with a downstroke.
Down-up, down on every beat. E, G, A and C, with the roots on the low E string: the open string, then frets 3, 5 and 8.
Each bar ends on a chord and the next bar starts on the new root half a beat later. Cut the chord a little short and move on it, so the first short note of the new bar is not late.
exercises.coachLine: Every attack is timed, chord and muted note alike, and the evenness is reported. A chord's pitch is not checked; the mute and the strokes are yours to judge.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?

variants.label: A string
variants.purpose: A, C, D and F under the reverse gallop, a bar each. The short notes are muted on the root, and on beats 2 and 4 the long note is the chord.
howTo: Count '1 e and, 2 e and'. Beats 1 and 3 are short-short-long on the muted root. On beats 2 and 4 the long note is the chord: lift the palm and strike both strings with a downstroke.
Down-up, down on every beat. A, C, D and F, with the roots on the A string: the open string, then frets 3, 5 and 8.
Each bar ends on a chord and the next bar starts on the new root half a beat later. Cut the chord a little short and move on it, so the first short note of the new bar is not late.
The low E string is not played. Begin every stroke on the A string and let the palm keep the low E string quiet.

exercises.title: Two beats a chord
exercises.purpose: The chords now change twice a bar: E and G in bar 1, A and C in bar 2. Each chord gets one gallop, with the chord as its long note, and one reverse gallop on the root.
howTo: Say it first: '1, and a, 2 e and, 3, and a, 4 e and'. The chord is on beats 1 and 3, and every other note is the muted root.
Down, down-up, then down-up, down. The last note before each change is an eighth note on the root: move on it.
From C at fret 8 back to E is the longest move. E needs only the first finger, on fret 2 of the A string, so let go of the C shape early and drop to it.
exercises.coachLine: Every attack is timed, chord and muted note alike, and the evenness is reported. A chord's pitch is not checked; the mute and the strokes are yours to judge.

variants.label: A string
variants.purpose: The chords now change twice a bar: A and C in bar 1, D and F in bar 2. Each chord gets one gallop, with the chord as its long note, and one reverse gallop on the root.
howTo: Say it first: '1, and a, 2 e and, 3, and a, 4 e and'. The chord is on beats 1 and 3, and every other note is the muted root.
Down, down-up, then down-up, down. The last note before each change is an eighth note on the root: move on it.
From F at fret 8 back to A is the longest move. A needs only the first finger, on fret 2 of the D string, so let go of the F shape early and drop to it.
The low E string is not played. Begin every stroke on the A string and let the palm keep the low E string quiet.

exercises.title: Four chords with the band
exercises.purpose: Four bars over a hard rock groove in E minor: E, G, A and C, a bar each. In the E, G and A bars the chord lands on beats 1 and 3, with a gallop after the first and a reverse gallop after the second. The C bar has its chord on beat 1 and again on beat 4, held for a beat.
howTo: Bars 1 to 3, on E, G and A: chord and two short notes, a gallop, chord and two short notes, a reverse gallop. Bar 4, on C: chord and two short notes, a gallop, a reverse gallop, and the C chord held on beat 4.
The band changes chord on beat 1 of every bar. Land your chord with it, and keep every muted note on that chord's root.
Back to bar 1: the held C chord is where the hand moves. Let it ring short; E needs only the first finger, on fret 2 of the A string.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Every attack is timed against it and the evenness is reported. A chord's pitch is not checked, and the mute and the strokes are yours to judge. Direct input or headphones make the timing fair.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Triplets, bursts and tremolo
steps.goal: Chug in triplets, fire a six-note burst into a chord, and tremolo-pick a melody on one string.
steps.why: Three more tools of the fast riff. Triplet chugs are the swing of doom and thrash alike. A burst of sextuplets into a chord is a drum fill on the guitar. Tremolo picking turns a slow melody into a wall of sound. All three depend on a relaxed alternating wrist at speed.
howTo: Triplets alternate strictly, so every other beat starts on an upstroke. Accent the first note of each beat either way.
A burst is one flick of six strokes, aimed at the note after it. Rest the hand on the chord.
For tremolo, make the stroke as small as you can and let the wrist stay loose. Tension is what stops it.
steps.payoff: A tremolo-picked melody in E minor, and bursts that land on their chord.

exercises.title: The triplet chug
exercises.purpose: Two bars of muted triplets on an open low string, the low E or the A, with the first note of each beat let out.
howTo: Count '1-trip-let, 2-trip-let'. Strict down-up, so beats 2 and 4 start on an upstroke.
Make the accent on the upstroke beats as strong as on the downstroke ones.
exercises.coachLine: I check that the first note of each beat was louder, roughly, and how even the triplets were.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.
Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: A burst into a chord
exercises.purpose: Six muted notes in one beat, then a power chord held for a beat. E, G, E and A.
howTo: Sextuplets: six to the click, down-up from a downstroke. The chord lands on the next beat with a downstroke.
Let the hand go soft while the chord rings, and set the fretting hand for the next chord.
exercises.coachLine: I time the six notes and the chord after them. Above the middle rungs, evenness is the number to trust.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: A tremolo melody
exercises.purpose: A slow E minor melody on the A string with every note picked four times: the melody moves once a beat and the pick never stops.
howTo: Sixteenths, strict down-up, no palm mute: let it ring. First finger on fret 7, third on 9, little finger on 10; the hand moves up two frets for bar 2, with the first finger on 9.
Change note exactly on the beat. The fretting hand is slow and the picking hand is fast; don't let one infect the other.

steps.title: Pedal-tone riffs
steps.goal: Play a melody on the A and D strings against a muted open low E, in sixteenths, without the pedal ringing or the melody choking.
steps.why: A pedal riff is two parts on one guitar: a muted low note that keeps returning and a melody above it. The pick has to leave the low string, cross one or two strings, and come back, in time, and the palm has to mute one string while the other rings.
howTo: Strict alternate picking. The melody notes fall on different strokes as the pattern turns, so don't try to make them all downstrokes.
Keep the palm on the low E string only. Roll the hand slightly so the A and D strings are free.
On a skip to the D string, the pick travels over the A string in a small arc. Don't lift the forearm.
steps.payoff: A riff where a melody on two strings dances over a chugging low E.

exercises.title: Melody on the A string
exercises.purpose: E, F# and G on the A string, each followed by two muted open E notes: groups of three sixteenths that roll across the beat, until the last beat, where melody and pedal take turns.
howTo: First finger on fret 7, third on 9, little finger on 10. One melody note, two pedal notes.
The melody notes ring and the open E is muted. Keep the strokes alternating through every crossing.

exercises.title: Melody on the D string

howTo: The same three fingers on the same frets, one string higher. Rest a spare finger on the A string so it can't ring.
The skip makes the pick's journey longer. Slow down until the pedal notes are as even as before.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.

exercises.title: Melody on both strings
exercises.purpose: The melody now jumps between the A and D strings over the same pedal: fourths and thirds in the tune, a crossing and a skip in every beat.
howTo: Bar 1 climbs: the A string note, then the same fret on the D string. Bar 2 comes back down with the D string first: fret 9, then the A string's 10, the D string's 7, the A string's 9, and both 7s to finish.
In bar 1 each pair is one finger: lay it flat across the A and D strings and pick one string at a time.

steps.title: Pedal riffs from the A string
steps.goal: Play a melody on the D and G strings against a muted open A string, in sixteenths, and change the pedal from the open A string to the open low E string on a bar line.
steps.why: Every pedal riff so far has stood on the open low E string. The open A string can be the low note just as well, and the whole figure moves one string higher with it: the same three fingers on the same frets, the same groups of three sixteenths. The melody notes are now A, B and C on the D string and D, E and F on the G string, and with A as the low note the riff is in A minor. For the picking hand, the palm has to mute the A string and leave the D and G strings free, and the low E string lies next to the pick without being played. In the last riff the pedal itself changes string and the melody goes with it, down to E and G on the A string.
howTo: Strict alternate picking, as in the pedal riffs on the low E string. In the groups of three the melody notes fall on a downstroke and an upstroke in turn, so do not try to make them all downstrokes.

Lay the side of the picking hand on the A string where it leaves the bridge. It rests on the low E string too, and that keeps the low E string quiet. Roll the hand a little so the D and G strings are free to ring.
The fretting hand stays at fret 7 for the whole Step: first finger on fret 7, third on fret 9, little finger on fret 10, on whichever string the melody is on.
On a skip to the G string, the pick travels over the D string in a small arc. Do not lift the forearm.
steps.payoff: A four-bar riff in A minor whose low note drops from the open A string to the open low E string and comes back.

exercises.title: Pedal on the A, melody on the D string

howTo: Sixteenth notes, strict down-up. One melody note and two pedal notes, four times; then one of each, twice, to fill the bar.

First finger on fret 7, third on fret 9, little finger on fret 10, all on the D string. Bar 1 is frets 7, 10, 9, 7, then 9 and 10. Bar 2 is frets 9, 7, 9, 10, then 9 and 7. Keep the fingers arched so no fingertip touches the A string.
The melody rings and the open A string is muted. The low E string is not played: the palm rests on it and keeps it quiet.

exercises.title: Melody on the G string

howTo: Sixteenth notes, strict down-up. The same three fingers on the same frets, one string higher. Bar 1 is frets 9, 10, 9, 7, then 9 and 10. Bar 2 is frets 9, 7, 9, 10, then 9 and 7.

Bar 1 climbs: frets 7, 9 and 10 on the D string, then frets 7 and 9 on the G string, and fret 7 again. Bar 2 comes down from the top: frets 10, 9 and 7 on the G string, then frets 10, 9 and 7 on the D string.
From the D string the pedal is the next string. From the G string the pick skips the D string on the way to the pedal and on the way back. Keep the pedal notes even through both.

exercises.title: The pedal changes string
exercises.purpose: Four bars in A minor. Bars 1 and 2 stand on the muted open A string, with the melody on the D and G strings. On the bar line into bar 3 the pedal drops to the muted open low E string, and the melody drops with it, to the A and D strings.
howTo: Sixteenth notes, strict down-up, the same groups in every bar: three, three, three, three, two and two.
Bar 1: frets 7, 9, 10 and 9 on the D string, fret 7 on the G string, fret 10 on the D string. Bar 2: frets 9 and 7 on the G string, then frets 10, 9, 7 and 9 on the D string.

Bar 3, over the open low E string: frets 7 and 10 on the A string, fret 7 on the D string, fret 10 on the A string, then frets 9 and 7 on the D string. Bar 4: frets 10, 9 and 7 on the D string, then frets 10, 7 and 10 on the A string.
The fretting hand never moves: first finger on fret 7, third on fret 9, little finger on fret 10.

At the change the palm rolls back. In bars 3 and 4 it mutes the low E string only, because the A string now carries melody and has to ring. Going back to bar 1 it covers the A string again. From the D string the pick now skips the A string: let the tip of the fretting finger lean against it, as it did against the D string.

steps.title: Chugs with holes in them
steps.goal: Play sixteenth-note riffs where some of the sixteenths are silent, so the riff starts and stops inside the beat.
steps.why: Modern heavy riffs are as much silence as sound: a burst of chugs, a hole, a chord, another hole. The holes are what make it heavy, and they only work if the strings are completely dead in them and the next note comes in exactly on its sixteenth.
howTo: The picking hand swings in sixteenths the whole time, down-up, and only touches the string on the written notes.
In a rest, the palm presses down a little harder and the fretting hand relaxes on the strings. Nothing rings.
Count '1 e and a' out loud at the first rung and say the played syllables louder.
steps.payoff: A stop-start riff that sounds like a machine switching on and off.

exercises.title: Two on, one off
exercises.purpose: Chug, chug, rest, in sixteenths: a three-sixteenth figure that rolls across the beat, on one muted low string, with two fretted eighths, not muted, to end the second bar.
howTo: Count the sixteenths '1 2 3, 1 2 3' and play on 1 and 2. Four times, then three chugs and a rest to fill the bar. In bar 2 the two eighths take the place of the three chugs and the rest.
The hand keeps swinging down-up, so the figure starts on a downstroke, then an upstroke, in turn.
exercises.coachLine: I time each chug against where it is written. A sound in a rest counts as an extra note.

exercises.title: Chord, hole, burst
exercises.purpose: A power chord on the beat, half a beat of silence, four muted sixteenths, another hole, a chord off the beat. Two bars, E, G and A.
howTo: Bar 1: E chord on 1, rest, four chugs on beat 2, rest, G chord on the 'and' of 3, two chugs and half a beat of rest.
Kill each chord with both hands. The chugs after a hole start exactly on the beat, not a hair before.
exercises.coachLine: I time every attack, chord and chug alike. A chord's pitch is not something I check.

exercises.title: A gallop with holes
exercises.purpose: A gallop, then sixteenths with the first and last one missing, then open notes on frets 3, 5 and 6 with a single chug between them. E blues on one string.
howTo: Bar 1: '1, and a, (2) e and, 3, a, 4'. The open notes on frets 3 and 5 are eighths; the single chug before beat 4 is on the 'a'.
First finger on fret 3, third on 5, little finger on 6: one finger per fret, and a real stretch this low on the neck.

steps.title: A riff in two parts
steps.goal: Play an eight-bar riff made of a pedal-tone part and a gallop-and-chord part, each part alone and then the two joined without a gap.
steps.why: A song puts riffs one after another: one part runs for four bars, another answers it, and the change has to arrive on the bar line. The two parts here ask different things. The pedal part is alternate-picked sixteenths with the hand at fret 7. The gallop part is down, down-up, with chords at the first frets. Neither is new. Holding one for four bars and then changing hand position and strokes in time is the work.
howTo: Learn each part by itself first. Part one is a pedal riff: a melody on the next two strings at frets 7, 9 and 10 over a muted open low string, strict down-up.
Part two is the gallop on the same open string with three power chords near the nut: down, down-up, and the chord in place of the long note.
At the join the fretting hand travels between fret 7 and the first frets. Both parts end on notes of the open string, and that is when the hand moves.
The first version is on the low E string; other Takes play the same frets one string higher, over the open A string.
steps.payoff: An eight-bar riff whose two parts follow each other without a seam.

howTo: Strict down-up. A group of three is one melody note and two muted open E notes; a group of two is one of each. The melody rings and the open string is muted.

First finger on fret 7, third on fret 9, little finger on fret 10. Bars 1 and 3 stay on the A string: frets 7, 9, 10, then 9, 7, 9. Bar 2 is frets 7, 9, 10 on the A string, then frets 7, 9, 7 on the D string.
Where fret 7 comes on both strings, across the bar line into bar 3, lay the first finger flat over the A and D strings; do not hop it.
Bar 4 comes down the A string, frets 10, 9, 7, then 9 and 7, and ends on four open E notes, a whole beat of them.

exercises.purpose: The whole riff: four bars of the pedal part, four bars of the gallop part, and round again. Eight bars at one tempo, with the change of part on a bar line.

Back to bar 1: bar 8 ends on a gallop on the open string, after the G chord. Move up during it, so the first finger is on fret 7 of the A string for the first note.
The tempo is set by the pedal part. The gallop part will feel slow at it: keep it exactly that slow.

steps.title: The band, and a full minute
steps.goal: Hold a galloping riff over a rock band for four bars, and keep downstrokes and gallops going for sixty seconds.
steps.why: A riff is played for minutes, not bars. Downpicking at speed is a stamina skill, the picking arm tires long before the fingers do, and the first sign is the time drifting late. A band behind you makes the same demand a different way: the riff has to lock to the kick drum.
howTo: For the minute-long takes, choose a rung about 20% below your clean tempo. It should feel easy for the first ten seconds.
Keep the shoulder down and the grip on the pick light. If the forearm locks, the set is over.
Stop at any pain in the hand, wrist or forearm. A tired forearm is one thing and pain is another; pain ends the set.
steps.payoff: A four-bar riff that sits on a band, and a minute of downstrokes that ends as tight as it began.

exercises.title: A riff with the band
exercises.purpose: Four bars in E minor over a hard rock groove: gallops on E with a climbing answer, then the gallop moved to G and to A.
howTo: Bars 1 and 2 are on the open low E string, with answers on frets 3, 5 and 6. Bar 3 gallops on fret 3, muted, and bar 4 on the open A string.
Listen to the kick drum. Your long notes land with it.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: A minute of downstrokes
exercises.purpose: Muted eighths on one low string, every one a downstroke, for sixty seconds. The classic thrash endurance test, at a tempo you choose.
howTo: Eighth notes, all down, with frets 3 and 5 at the end of each bar to mark it.
When it starts to burn, make the stroke smaller before you slow down. If it still burns, stop.
exercises.coachLine: I check that the time holds to the end of the minute. Whether every stroke was down is yours to say.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

Long unbroken playing, especially high-gain, can drown out where each note starts, so the app may stop hearing you. Unproven either way; if the app says it did not catch enough, believe that before you doubt your hands.

selfCheck: Were they all downstrokes, to the last bar?

exercises.title: A minute of gallops
exercises.purpose: The gallop on one low string for sixty seconds, with a fretted gallop at the end of each bar.
howTo: Down, down-up, without a break. The two short notes are the first thing to blur when the arm tires.
Breathe, and drop the shoulder at a bar line if it has crept up.
exercises.coachLine: I check that the time holds to the end of the minute and that the short notes are still there.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

Long unbroken playing, especially high-gain, can drown out where each note starts, so the app may stop hearing you. Unproven either way; if the app says it did not catch enough, believe that before you doubt your hands.

steps.difficultyException: Mostly gallops and eighth notes with hardly a string crossing, after an eight-bar riff that crosses strings in sixteenths, so the number falls though the attacks come about as fast. The demand is a band to lock to and sixty seconds without the time drifting, and the metric does not count stamina or listening.

steps.title: A verse and a chorus, with the band
steps.goal: Play a four-bar verse riff and a four-bar chorus riff, each alone, then verse, verse, chorus, chorus as sixteen bars with a band, keeping the tempo through every change of part.
steps.why: A song is longer than a riff, and it changes feel as it goes. The verse riff here is tight: muted, low and busy, and it stays on one chord. The chorus opens up: power chords that ring, a new chord in every bar, and a rhythm with far fewer notes in it. No technique here is new: the gallop, eighth notes let out of the mute that answer it, and power chords. Only the verse's fingering is: the hand sits one fret lower than in the earlier single-note riffs, first finger on fret 2. The work is keeping your place in sixteen bars, and the change: on one bar line the palm comes off the strings and the strokes get bigger, and on another they go back to small and muted, at the same tempo.
howTo: Learn each part by itself first, with the click. The verse is the gallop on the muted open low E string with short answers on the A string. The chorus is four power chords, one to a bar: E, C, G and D.
The verse is down, down-up, with the palm on the low E string. The chorus is all downstrokes, palm off the strings, each stroke carried through two strings.
Into the chorus, lift the palm and let the first chord ring for its full two beats. The tempo has not changed, only how much you play: count through the long chord and do not rush it.
Back into the verse, bring the palm down before the first note, so the gallop starts muted.

With the band, the chord stays E5 through the whole verse and the first bar of the chorus, then C5, G5 and D5, a bar each. Nothing in the chords tells you the chorus has come, so count the bars in fours.
steps.payoff: Sixteen bars of rhythm guitar with a band: two verses, two choruses, and the change of feel on the bar line.

exercises.title: The verse riff
exercises.purpose: Four bars in E minor: gallops on the muted open low E string, with a two-note answer on the A string in each of the first three bars and a four-note run down in the last.
howTo: Bars 1 to 3: two gallops, two eighth notes on the A string, and one more gallop. Count '1, and a, 2, and a, 3 and, 4, and a'. Down, down-up for each gallop and two downstrokes for the answer.

The answers are frets 2 and 3 in bars 1 and 3, B and C, and frets 5 and 3 in bar 2, D and C. First finger on fret 2, second on fret 3, little finger on fret 5. Lift the palm so they ring. The first finger stays over fret 2 of the A string throughout: it is already in place for the E chord of the chorus.
Bar 4: one gallop, then four eighth notes running down, frets 5, 3 and 2 on the A string and fret 3 on the low E string under the second finger, and one gallop to end the bar.
exercises.coachLine: Every note is timed, and after the take the notes are checked against the written ones. The mute and the strokes are yours to judge.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?

exercises.title: The chorus riff
exercises.purpose: Four bars, a power chord to each: E, C, G and D. Every bar has the same rhythm, a chord held for two beats, a chord for one beat and two eighth notes, and every chord rings.
howTo: Count '1, 2, 3, 4 and' and play on 1, on 3, on 4 and on its 'and'. All downstrokes, palm off the strings, through two strings only.

E is the open low E string and fret 2 of the A string. C is fret 3 of the A string and fret 5 of the D string. G is the same two frets one string lower: fret 3 of the low E string and fret 5 of the A string. D is fret 5 of the A string and fret 7 of the D string.
First finger on the lower string and third finger two frets up on the next string, for C, G and D. E needs the first finger alone.
The fretting hand moves on the last eighth note of the bar. Let that chord be short and land the next one on the click.
For C and D, begin the stroke on the A string, so the low E string stays quiet.
exercises.coachLine: A chord is one attack: it is timed and counted, and its pitch is not checked. Whether both strings rang, and no others, is yours to judge.
selfCheck: Did both strings of every chord ring, and no others, with only the last chord of each bar cut short for the move?

exercises.title: Verse into chorus, with the band
exercises.purpose: One verse and one chorus, eight bars over a hard rock groove in E minor, and round again. The feel changes twice in every pass: into the chorus at bar 5 and back into the verse at bar 1.
howTo: Bars 1 to 4 are the verse riff: muted gallops, down, down-up. Bars 5 to 8 are the chorus: E, C, G and D, all downstrokes, ringing.
Into bar 5: bar 4 ends on a gallop on the open low E string. Lift the palm after its last note and strike the E chord with the band, first finger on fret 2 of the A string.
Back to bar 1: bar 8 ends on two D chords, at frets 5 and 7. The verse starts with two gallops on the open string, and that is when the hand comes back down to fret 2. Bring the palm down first.

The band holds E under the whole verse and stays on it for the first bar of the chorus, then changes with you to C, G and D, a bar each. The chorus does not arrive with a new chord: you make it arrive by opening up.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Every attack is timed against it, in both parts, and the evenness is reported. No pitch is checked in this one, neither the chords nor the verse notes; the mute and the strokes are yours to judge. Direct input or headphones make the timing fair.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?
Did the change of part arrive on time both ways, into bar 5 and back to bar 1?

exercises.title: Verse, verse, chorus, chorus
exercises.purpose: The whole form with the band: the verse twice, then the chorus twice, sixteen bars at one tempo. Nothing in it is new. Knowing where you are in sixteen bars is the lesson.
howTo: Bars 1 to 8 are the verse riff played twice. Bars 9 to 16 are the chorus played twice: E, C, G and D, then E, C, G and D again.

Count the fours as they go by: verse one, verse two, chorus one, chorus two. The run down marks the last bar of each verse. After the first run the verse starts again; after the second, at bar 9, the chorus starts.
At bar 9, lift the palm and let the E chord ring for its two beats. Between the two choruses, from D back to E, the hand drops from fret 5 to fret 2 on the last eighth note of bar 12.
After bar 16 the form starts again from the verse. Bring the palm down before the first gallop.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Sixteen bars are timed without a break, every attack in both parts, and the evenness is reported. No pitch is checked in this one, neither the chords nor the verse notes; the mute and the strokes are yours to judge. Direct input or headphones make the timing fair.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did the muted notes thud with a clear pitch, neither ringing open nor choked dead?
Did both changes arrive on time, into the chorus at bar 9 and back into the verse at bar 1?
Did the chorus chords ring and the verse stay muted, every time round?

steps.difficultyException: The chorus is four attacks to a bar and the verse is a gallop at the tempo the Step before held for a minute, so the note rate falls. The demand is sixteen bars in one take and a change of feel on a bar line, from muted gallops to ringing chords and back, which a note-rate metric does not count.

levels.title: Beginner: the chug
levels.summary: Palm-muted downstrokes, two-note power chords, the two together in a riff, and the same chug and chords with their roots on the A string.

startHereIf: You can play eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM.
You've never practised palm muting, or your muted notes come out uneven.
You can't yet change between two power chords in time.

warmups.purpose: Muted eighths on one string: the root and its minor third, then the fourth and fifth a hand higher. A different key and string each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. All downstrokes, palm-muted. The hand moves up five frets at the bar line and back.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

levels.title: Intermediate: the gallop
levels.summary: The gallop, the reverse gallop, continuous alternate-picked sixteenths with accents, and both gallops under chords that change every bar and then every two beats, ending with a band.

startHereIf: You can play palm-muted eighths in downstrokes at 100 BPM, even and all the same weight.

Your gallops smear, or you can't switch between a gallop and straight sixteenths.

levels.title: Advanced: speed and stamina
levels.summary: Triplet chugs, sextuplet bursts and tremolo picking, pedal-tone riffs across strings, first over the open low E string and then over the open A string, stop-start riffs with silent sixteenths, an eight-bar riff in two parts, a riff over a band and a full minute, then a verse and a chorus as a sixteen-bar form with the band.

Your riffs fall apart when they leave the low string, or your picking arm tires before a song is over.
